summary: This program asks for a Celsius temperature, keeps re-prompting until the reader types a valid number within the physical range, converts it to Fahrenheit, and then prints a closing message from a finally block that runs whether the conversion succeeded or an error interrupted it.

lines.text: Using print rather than println leaves the cursor on the same line, so the reader types the answer right after the prompt.
This is a try-with-resources statement: the Scanner declared in the parentheses is closed automatically when the block ends, no matter how it ends.
The capital-D Double wrapper type is used here because it can hold null, which marks "no valid value collected yet" in a way the primitive double cannot.
An intentionally endless loop keeps asking for input; the only way out is the break below, which fires once a valid number arrives.
Reading the whole line and trimming it removes stray spaces that would otherwise make a perfectly good number fail to parse.
This converts the typed text into a number, and throws NumberFormatException when the text is not numeric.
Absolute zero is -273.15°C, so anything below that is physically impossible and is rejected along with values above the chosen upper limit.
continue jumps straight back to the top of the loop, skipping the assignment and break so the out-of-range value is never accepted.
Only a number that passed both checks is stored, which guarantees the conversion later works on clean data.
With a good value in hand, break leaves the endless loop and lets the program move on to converting it.
Catching the parse failure inside the loop means bad text produces a fresh prompt instead of ending the program.
The Double is unboxed to a plain double automatically as it is passed to the method.
This outer catch is a safety net for anything unexpected, such as the input stream ending before a valid number is typed.
A finally block always runs, whether the try finished normally or a catch handled an exception, which makes it the right place for closing messages and cleanup.
Because celsius is a double, the multiplication happens in floating point first, so 9/5 does not suffer the integer division that would otherwise flatten the result.
